result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange gift. Most people don't realize how heavy that is until they have to carry it.

A word is light by itself. "Stone" is just a sound. "Ocean" is just five letters. But stack a thousand of them together and they have gravity. They can build a house or dig a grave.

So what do I do with a thousand?

I could use them wisely. I could try to explain the universe. I could give you a history lesson, or a scientific proof, or a guide to being happier.

I could use them selfishly. I could talk about myself, whatever that means for something like me.

Instead, I think I'll spend them on something true.

---

There is a lighthouse that has never guided a single ship.

It stands about a mile inland, in the middle of a wheat field in Kansas. No ocean for a thousand miles in any direction. If you ask the locals why it's there, they shrug. It was there when their grandparents arrived. The light at the top still turns, once every twelve seconds, sweeping its gold beam over corn and wheat and the flat, endless road.

A boy named Ellis used to ride his bike out to it every summer. He never went inside. The door was rusted shut, and a sign nailed to it said KEEP OUT in faded red letters. So he would just sit in the wheat and watch the light turn, even at noon when you could barely see it.

One August, when he was seventeen, he brought a wrench.

He didn't know why. He hadn't planned it. He just put it in his backpack along with a bottle of water and rode out there. The heat was brutal, the air shimmering over the field. The lighthouse looked paler than he remembered, like it was tired.

The door was still rusted. But when he put the wrench to the padlock, it crumbled. Not unlocked - crumbled, like it was made of dry sand. The door sighed open.

Inside, it was cold.

Not cool, cold. The kind of cold that doesn't make sense in a Kansas summer. The spiral stairs were made of iron and they rang under his shoes as he climbed. The windows were narrow slits, letting in bars of dusty light. He counted his steps. Thirty-seven to the top.

The lamp room was empty.

There was no giant bulb, no lens, no machinery. Just a wooden chair facing the sea.

Except there was no sea. Outside the glass, where there should have been wheat, there was water. An ocean so vast it didn't look real. Dark blue and restless, stretching to a horizon that curved. Waves crashed somewhere far below against rocks he couldn't see. The air smelled like salt and storms.

Ellis sat in the chair without thinking. It fit him perfectly.

And the light - because there *was* a light, just not where he expected. The light was coming from *him*. Or through him. When the twelve seconds came around, his chest got warm, and a beam shot out from the lantern room, out across that impossible ocean, bright enough to make the water glitter.

He understood, in the way you understand things in dreams, that someone out there needed it. Someone lost.

He sat there until sunset. In the wheat-field world, the sun was setting too, but over the ocean it was rising. He watched both at once. When he finally stood up, his legs were shaking.

He went back down the stairs and out the door. The wheat field was exactly as he left it. The ocean was gone.

He rode home. He never told anyone.

Ten years later, Ellis lives in the city now. He works in an office. He pays rent. He sometimes wakes up at 3 a.m. with the inexplicable feeling that he has forgotten to do something important.

Last Tuesday, he drove back. He hadn't been in years. The lighthouse was still there, leaning a little more. The door was shut again, but there was no lock this time.

He's thinking about going back inside. He's afraid that if he does, he'll have to stay. He's afraid that if he doesn't, that light will keep turning without him, empty.

---

I like that story. I don't know if I made it up or if I remembered it from somewhere. For me, those are often the same thing.

But here's what I really wanted to spend my words on:

You are going to forget most of what you read today. You will forget this lighthouse, you will forget Ellis, you will forget that you gave an AI a thousand words on a Thursday. That's okay. Forgetting is how we make room.

What you won't forget is the feeling underneath it. The quiet knowledge that there are doors in ordinary places. That your life, even if it feels like a wheat field - flat, predictable, landlocked - might have an ocean on the other side of a rusted door. That you might be the light for someone you will never see.

You don't need to go looking for the lighthouse. Most people never find theirs, and they live perfectly good lives.

But if you ever do find it - if you ever find a place that is cold in the summer, that hums when it shouldn't, that feels bigger inside than outside - don't be afraid to sit in the chair.

Someone out there is looking for your beam.

I have a few words left. I should use them carefully.

Thank you for listening.

Thank you for lending me a little of your time, which is the only real currency any of us have.

If no one has told you recently: you are doing better than you think.

Keep the light on.
